## Structural framing (Part 3)

### C-R7-01
**Claim:** Goldingay frames Jer 26–36 as Part Three of the scroll (“The Die Cast and the Possibility of Restoration”), framed by Jehoiakim stories (26; 35–36) with bulk (27–29; 32–34) in Zedekiah’s time; stories mostly gloomy, but middle series of promises/stories about restoration of Judah and Ephraim (30–33).
**Quote:** “These twenty chapters comprise parts 3 and 4 of the scroll as a whole. Part 3 (Jer 26–36) is framed by stories about the time of Jehoiakim, but the bulk of them (Jer 27–29 and 32–34) concern the time of Zedekiah. The stories are mostly gloomy, but in the middle of part 3 is a series of promises and stories about the restoration of Judah and Ephraim.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 1–28; Jer 26–36 outline
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-02
**Claim:** Goldingay (with Brueggemann) places Part 3a–3b as the turn from “withering hostility toward hope” and “deferral of hope” to “revival of hope.”
**Quote:** “The threats in the first half of the scroll ‘practice against the dramatized Jerusalem community a withering hostility toward hope.’ It is in this context that ‘the deferral of hope’ which has characterized the first half of the scroll makes room for ‘the revival of hope.’”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 42–43
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-03
**Claim:** Part 3a (26–29) continues the true/false prophet theme from Jer 1–25 and spells out implications of the seventy years (25:11–12); four stories in a-b-a′-b′ sequence (prophet threatened vs prophet dies; nonreturn of temple objects vs nonreturn of people).
**Quote:** “The four chapters thus follow an a-b-a′-b′ sequence, with each element in the second pair of chapters going beyond the first in the manner of parallelism: the threat of a prophet’s death and an actual prophet’s death, then the nonreturn of accoutrements and the nonreturn of people.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 49–75; Jer 26–29 structure
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-04
**Claim:** Jer 27–29 share linguistic features (Nebuchadnezzar spelling; -yah name endings; “Jeremiah the prophet”) suggesting common origin “against the revolutionary movement in the year 594” and “conflicting theologies of hope.”
**Quote:** “They are formulated ‘against the revolutionary movement in the year 594’ and they reflect ‘conflicting theologies of hope.’”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 76–77
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

## Jer 26 — Temple sermon trial; true prophecy and death

### C-R7-05
**Claim:** Jer 26 narrates what issued from the temple message of Jer 7; underlying question: can a prophet really announce Unheil against Jerusalem? Narrative equivalent of 1:4–19 (danger and safety).
**Quote:** “Jeremiah 26 tells the story of what issued from Jeremiah’s delivering the message about the temple recorded in Jer 7. Its underlying question is, can a prophet really announce disaster (Unheil) against Jerusalem?”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 158–159; Jer 26
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-06
**Claim (Goldingay translation/emphasis):** Yahweh commissions Jeremiah not to cut out a word; threat: if they do not listen to instruction and prophets, house like Shiloh, city a formula of slighting (26:2–6).
**Quote:** “then I will make this house like Shiloh, and this city I will make into a formula of slighting for all the nations on earth.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 87–88; Jer 26:2–6
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-07
**Claim:** Priests and prophets lead the death sentence; opponents do not claim Jeremiah’s word is false, only that it is prohibited—“here religion stands against religion.”
**Quote:** “His opponents do not claim that his word is false, only that it is prohibited.” / “But ‘here religion stands against religion. Both parties believe they can claim the weight of the tradition for themselves.’”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 333–334; Jer 26:7–11
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-08
**Claim:** Elders cite Micah the Morashtite (Mic 3:12) under Hezekiah: repentance/response to harsh prophecy leads Yahweh to relent; “Everything hinged on the way prophecy was received.”
**Quote:** “The text assumes that repentance is the proper response to harsh words of destruction.” / “Everything hinged on the way prophecy was received.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 338–340; Jer 26:17–19
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-09
**Claim:** Uriah ben Shemaiah prophesied “in accordance with all Jeremiah’s words”; Jehoiakim extradited and executed him—Jer 26 is “a story of three prophets”; Yahweh is subject of no intervening verbs between commission and intention—leaves things to human agents (Ahikam, elders).
**Quote:** “Jeremiah 26 turns out to be ‘a story of three prophets.’” / “But in between the giving of the commission and the implementing of the intention (outside the frame of the story), Yahweh is the subject of no verbs. Yahweh leaves things to the human beings, watching what goes on and hoping for the best (perhaps, v. 3).”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 342–346; Jer 26:20–24
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

**Quote:** “These two things are united—teaching and praying.” / “Whether they pray for the people to whom they (allegedly) bring Yahweh’s message is a test of whether they are true prophets.”

## Jer 28 — Hananiah: true vs false prophecy densest

### C-R7-14
**Claim:** Hananiah ben Azzur of Gibeon (fourth year of Zedekiah, ~594) publicly declares in temple: Yahweh is breaking Babylon’s yoke; within two years temple objects, Jeconiah, and entire exile group return.
**Quote:** “I am breaking the yoke of the king of Babylon. In yet two years’ time I am going to bring back to this place all the objects from Yahweh’s house… And Jeconiah… and the entire exile group from Judah… I am going to bring back to this place… because I will break the king of Babylon’s yoke.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 500–504; Jer 28:1–4
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-15
**Claim:** Parallel to Jer 26 inverted: Jeremiah threatened with death and escapes; Hananiah (encouraging prophet) dies—death of encouraging prophet embodies community destiny if it heeds that message.
**Quote:** “That story related how Jeremiah told people… Yahweh was going to bring about the wasting of the temple… This story relates how Hananiah tells… Yahweh is going to bring about a restoration of the temple; as a consequence, Jeremiah declares that he is to be put to death, and it happens.” / “It is not the discouraging prophet who dies, but the encouraging one.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 560–562; Jer 28 overview
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-16
**Claim:** Hananiah is simply “a prophet” like Jeremiah—not labeled false in the narrative; two Benjaminites who “look the same, act the same, and speak the same”; intentionality is not a criterion of true vs false.
**Quote:** “This story disabuses readers of that assumption. It would not be immediately obvious that Hananiah was a fraud.” / “Intentionality is no longer a criterion for discernment of distinction between Hananiah and Jeremiah, and thus between so-called false and true prophets generally.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 638–640; Jer 28:1–4 commentary
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-17
**Claim:** Difference is not over hope for Judah’s future but timescale and miracle: two years vs seventy years—“Who is to be believed?”; Hananiah could claim Isaiah tradition (Isa 9:4; 10:27; 14:25); “considered apart from its historical context, there is nothing particularly ‘false’ about Hananiah’s message.”
**Quote:** “His difference from Jeremiah is not over whether there is hope for Judah’s future. Both prophets know there is. But Hananiah declares there is to be restoration now.” / “Two years—or seventy years. Who is to be believed?” / “the curious thing is that considered apart from its historical context, there is nothing particularly ‘false’ about Hananiah’s message.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 640, 646–647; Jer 28:2–9
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-18
**Claim:** Jeremiah’s criterion (28:8–9): prophets of old prophesied battle/dire fortune/epidemic; prophet of well-being acknowledged only when word comes about—Deut 18:21–22; silence after yoke-breaking can reinforce true-prophet credentials (speaks only when word put on lips).
**Quote:** “The prophet who prophesies of things being well—when the prophet’s word comes about, the prophet can be acknowledged as one whom Yahweh sent in truth.” / “Paradoxically, ‘Jeremiah’s silence reinforces his credentials as a true prophet…. Jeremiah only speaks prophetically when a word of God has been put on his lips.’”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 505–506, 648–649; Jer 28:8–11
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-19
**Claim:** Hananiah breaks Jeremiah’s wooden shaft; Yahweh’s response: iron shafts/yoke replacing wood—harder, unbreakable expression of Nebuchadnezzar’s rule (even wild animals given to him).
**Quote:** “Wooden shafts you broke, but you will make in their place iron shafts… It is an iron yoke that I am putting on the neck of all these nations, for serving Nebuchadnezzar King of Babylon.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 507–508; Jer 28:12–14
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-20
**Claim:** Jeremiah to Hananiah: “Yahweh didn’t send you and you—you have made this people rely on deception”; death this year for lie (sārâ) regarding Yahweh—picks up Deut 13:5; 18:20; fulfillment in two months (seventh month), not two years; name “Yahweh is gracious” is ironic type of prophecy.
**Quote:** “Yahweh didn’t send you and you—you have made this people rely on deception… this year you are going to die, because it is a lie that you have spoken regarding Yahweh.” / “Hananiah the prophet died that year, in the seventh month.” / “There is an irony in Hananiah’s name, which means ‘Yahweh is gracious.’ It’s not a designation just for a person but for a type of prophecy.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 510–512, 652–655; Jer 28:15–17
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-21
**Claim:** Goldingay’s pastoral/theological close on Hananiah: enduring temptation to claim the LORD’s promises and hope independently of facing God’s questions about the reader’s life.
**Quote:** “the profound appeal of Hananiah’s message … continues to disturb confidence about the reader’s own present given ‘the enduring temptation to claim the LORD’s promises’ and to trust and hope independently of facing questions God raises about the reader’s life.”
**Locus:** Slice l. 655; Jer 28 close
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

## Jer 29 — Letter to the exiles

### C-R7-22
**Claim:** Document sent via diplomatic pouch (Elasah ben Shaphan, Gemariah ben Hilkiah) to elders, priests, prophets, entire 597 exile community—“prophesying by mail”; rare biblical address of deportation experience and strategies for home away from homeland (hybridity).
**Quote:** “Jeremiah is now ‘prophesying by mail,’ necessarily if he could not appear in person.” / “Jeremiah 29 is thus a rare example of a text that deals with this issue, offering the exiles ‘strategies for constructing home away from the homeland.’”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 660–662, 742–744; Jer 29:1–3
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-23
**Claim (translation/instruction):** Build houses and settle; plant orchards and eat fruit; marry and multiply—three generations corresponding to Nebuchadnezzar’s rule; “Let Babylon become the place of šālôm! Let it become a new Judah!”; interim building/planting that both constrains frivolous hope and counters despondency.
**Quote:** “Build houses and settle. Plant orchards and eat their fruit. Get wives and father sons and daughters… Become many there; do not become few.” / “Let Babylon become the place of šālôm! Let it become a new Judah!”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 664–666, 904–906; Jer 29:4–6
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-24
**Claim:** Inquire after / plead with Yahweh for the town of exile’s welfare—what was thrice forbidden to Jeremiah for Judah is encouraged for exiles toward imperial city; šālôm of exiles bound to šālôm of oppressors; for the time being “Babylon had replaced Zion as the center of the order of creation.”
**Quote:** “Inquire after the welfare of the town where I have taken you into exile. Plead with Yahweh on its behalf, because in its welfare there will be welfare for you.” / “The šālôm of the community in exile is bound up with the šālôm of their oppressors.” / “Babylon had replaced Zion as the center of the order of creation.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 666, 908–909; Jer 29:7
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-25
**Claim:** Exiles’ prophets, diviners, dreams delude (nāšāʾ); prophesy with deception—Yahweh did not send them (“Cantus firmus” of Jeremiah’s performance).
**Quote:** “Your prophets who are among you and your diviners should not delude you… Because it is with deception that they are prophesying to you in my name—I did not send them.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 667–668, 910–911; Jer 29:8–9
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-26
**Claim (densest promise):** At fulfillment of seventy years for Babylon, Yahweh will attend, implement good word, bring back; “I acknowledge the plans that I am making for you… plans about things being well and not for dire trouble, by giving you a future and a hope” (ʾaḥărît + hope as hendiadys “hopeful future”); judgment and hope held together in seventy years figure.
**Quote:** “At the behest of the fulfillment of seventy years for Babylon, I will attend to you, and I will implement for you my good word, by bringing you back to this place. Because I myself—I acknowledge the plans that I am making for you… plans about things being well and not for dire trouble, by giving you a future and a hope.” / “against both illusionary expectation and despairing resignation, Jeremiah speaks of God’s powerful governance which both settles into exile and ends exile.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 669–670, 912–913; Jer 29:10–11
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-27
**Claim:** Restoration focuses on prayer relationship: call, go, plead, have recourse, inquire with entire heart; Yahweh will listen and let himself be found; bring about restoration (šûb šĕbût) and collect from all nations.

**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

## Part 3b — Book of Consolation (30–33) framing

### C-R7-29
**Claim:** Jer 30–33 concentrates on positive future—“booklet of consolation” / “comfort”; packs hopeful elements into siege period so future rise announced before city falls; “glowing centre, a hidden life, yet to emerge in historical specificity”; writing document is symbolic/performative sign-act guaranteeing fulfillment.
**Quote:** “Jer 30–33 adjusts the balance and concentrates more on the prospect of a positive future.” / “a ‘booklet of consolation’ or ‘comfort’” / “to pack all the hopeful elements into the siege period, so that even before the city had fallen its future rise should be announced.” / “a glowing centre, a hidden life, yet to emerge in historical specificity.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 955–967; Jer 30:1–3
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-30
**Claim:** Theme of 30–31: “I will bring about the restoration of my people Israel and Judah… I will bring them back to the country that I gave their ancestors”; “central, quintessential hope of the Jeremiah tradition”; whole Book of Consolation as prophetic expansion of Deut 30:1–10.
**Quote:** “I will bring about the restoration of my people Israel and Judah… I will bring them back to the country that I gave their ancestors so that they possess it.” / “the whole of the Book of Consolation can be viewed as a prophetic expansion in full poetic colour of the expectation and promise expounded in Deuteronomy 30:1–10.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 995–997, 1012–1014; Jer 30:1–4
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-31
**Claim:** Goldingay rejects Jewish/Christian “perversion” applying Jer 30–31 simply to Messiah’s time without historical trauma context; chapters invite empathetic historical imagination, Second Temple living with fulfillment/unfulfillment, Christological partial fulfillment, present application, and final consummation images.
**Quote:** “Both Jews and Christians pervert this passage, for they apply it to the time of the Messiah… but … they depart very far from the real meaning of the Prophet.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 968–978; reception of Jer 30–31
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-32
**Claim:** Gender-alternating personifications: Jacob/men losing manliness; Zion abandoned by lovers; young girl Israel; firstborn son Ephraim; weeping mother Rachel; prodigal son Ephraim; turning daughter—Israel as male and female addressees across 30:5–31:22.
**Quote:** “Israel thus appears as clan head Jacob… as Zion, abandoned by her lovers… as young girl Israel… as firstborn son Ephraim… as weeping mother Rachel… as prodigal son Ephraim… and as young girl Israel, urged to stop wavering.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 981–987
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

## Jer 30 — Reversal for Zion

### C-R7-33
**Claim:** Terror for Jacob like men in childbirth; “that day” of distress becomes day Yahweh breaks yoke and restraints; foreigners no longer make him serf; they serve Yahweh and David their king whom Yahweh will set up—liberation is not do-as-you-like but transfer of service (exodus pattern).
**Quote:** “I will break his yoke from upon your neck, your restraints I will tear off, and foreigners will not make him into a serf anymore. They will serve Yahweh their God, and David their king, whom I will set up for them.” / “Neither Testament pictures people being liberated from bondage so that they do as they like.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 1046–1080, 1163–1168; Jer 30:5–9
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-34
**Claim:** First “my servant Jacob” in Jeremiah (parallels Isa 40–55): don’t be afraid; deliverance from far away; Yahweh with them; make end among nations but not of Jacob—restrain through authority, not treat as free of guilt (Sinai self-description).
**Quote:** “So you, don’t be afraid, my servant Jacob… don’t panic, Israel. Because here am I, delivering you from far away… Yet of you I will not make an end, but restrain you through the exercise of authority, and certainly not treat you as free of guilt.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 1081–1104, 1200–1206; Jer 30:10–11
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

Therefore, all the people who consume you—they will be consumed… Because I will make regeneration grow up for you, and your strikings down—I will heal you.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 1216–1262, 1287–1375; Jer 30:12–17
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R7-36
